corrections.form_value: Fifty-six Italian undergraduates (economics programs) read a short text and answered two analysis-and-evaluation questions and one creation question (a social media post of up to 800 characters). The paper calls the design quasi-experimental but states that students were randomly assigned to an experimental group that could use AI tools on the first two questions and a control group that worked without digital support throughout; neither group had AI for the creation question. The post was scored with a four-indicator rubric (0 to 12), and the two groups' Total_Create scores were compared.

confirmed: Read all 365 markdown lines and all 12 PDF pages, including the references; there are no appendices in this PDF. The journal header gives Anno 6 n. 1 (2026), and the title and three authors match the form (p. 1; references pp. 11–12).

The methods explicitly report random assignment of university students to experimental and control groups, with creative output scored afterward; has_randomized_people_study is true and the paper belongs in the two-screener pipeline (p. 3, Section 2.1; pp. 5–6, rubric and Table 1).

The source also calls the design quasi-experimental and cautions against strong causal inference; the form correctly flags this internal inconsistency, and the randomization procedure is not described (p. 1, abstract; p. 3, Section 2.1; pp. 9–10, Section 5).

Regular-coursework recruitment is reported, supporting the form's coursework setting for field_rct; the paper reports a people experiment rather than AI-versus-human output or a synthesis, so context_class = none is appropriate. Data collection used an online questionnaire (p. 4, Sections 2.2–2.3).
Table 1 analyzes 28 people in each arm, consistent with the stated 56-person sample; these are people, not ratings or texts, and the analyzed sample exceeds 50 (p. 4, Section 2.2; p. 6, Table 1).
The source states mean age 21, 45% first-year Economics and Data Analysis, 54% third-year Business Economics, and retention of one Master's student; no exclusions are described (p. 4, Section 2.2).

AI access differed only for the two Analysis and Evaluation questions preceding the creative post; after_ai is supported for the subsequent creation task, and no delayed follow-up is described (p. 3, Section 2.1; p. 5, Section 2.3).
The task requests a social media post of up to 800 characters with a title/slogan. The rubric has four indicators, each scored 0–3, with a maximum total of 12 (pp. 5–6, Section 2.3).

Both the reported string and one_line_finding reproduce the PDF's numbers: AI group N = 28, mean 8.21, SD 1.97; control N = 28, mean 7.64, SD 1.94; +0.57 points, p = .31, Cohen's d = 0.26, described as not statistically significant (p. 6, Table 1 and Section 3.2).

The A.S.K. module is reported through normative performance bands and a correlation with creative-post performance, without an AI-arm contrast or clear timing relative to AI exposure; it is not a separate experiment (p. 5, Section 2.3; pp. 7–8, Sections 3.3 and 3.5).

No AI model, preregistration, supplement, or data/code availability link is specified in the full document; this is one empirical study, so the empty synthesis fields are appropriate (pp. 1–12, especially Sections 2–3).
summary: The paper reports random assignment to AI access during analysis before an unassisted creative post, with 56 people analyzed, so it belongs in the two-screener pipeline. The main statistics match the PDF; four corrections concern the unreported assignment-stage count, unsupported rater expertise and sample description, and an overlong quotation.
